pack.description: Listen to a Conversation — short two-speaker campus conversations, two questions each.
pack.copyright_policy: Original synthetic content. No operational ETS item copied.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and an equipment desk assistant.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Hi, I came to pick up the camera I reserved for my media project.

audio.speaker: Assistant
audio.text: Let me check. Your reservation starts tomorrow morning.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Really? I thought I selected Thursday.

audio.speaker: Assistant
audio.text: Today is Thursday, but the form shows Friday at nine.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: That's a problem. We're filming an interview this afternoon.

audio.speaker: Assistant
audio.text: The reserved cameras are all checked out, but I have a basic model that nobody booked. It doesn't have the external microphone input, though.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: We can record the audio separately. I'll take it.

questions.stem: Why does the student visit the equipment desk?
options: To return a damaged camera
To collect equipment for a project
To change the topic of a media project
To reserve a microphone for Friday
questions.explanation: He came "to pick up the camera I reserved for my media project".

questions.stem: What will the student probably do?
options: Cancel the interview
Wait until Friday
Use a simpler camera and record sound separately
Buy a new microphone
questions.explanation: He accepts the basic model and says they can record the audio separately.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and her academic advisor.

audio.speaker: Advisor
audio.text: So, you wanted to talk about adding a second major?

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Yes, in statistics. I've taken three courses already and really enjoyed them.

audio.speaker: Advisor
audio.text: That's a good start. The catch is that two of the required courses are only offered in the spring, and they clash with your biology lab.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Could I take the lab in the summer instead?

audio.speaker: Advisor
audio.text: Possibly. The summer section fills fast, though, so you'd want to register the day enrollment opens.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Okay, I'll set a reminder. And I'll fill out the major declaration form today.

questions.stem: What problem does the advisor point out?
options: The student has not taken enough statistics courses
Two required courses conflict with the student's lab schedule
Statistics is not offered as a second major
The summer biology lab has been cancelled
questions.explanation: Two spring-only courses "clash with your biology lab".

questions.stem: What does the advisor imply about the summer lab?
options: It is easier than the spring lab
Getting a place may be difficult
It does not count toward the degree
It is only open to statistics majors
questions.explanation: "Fills fast… register the day enrollment opens" implies limited places.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between two students in a dormitory.

audio.speaker: Jake
audio.text: Hey, are you using the kitchen tonight? I was going to cook for my study group.

audio.speaker: Lina
audio.text: I was planning to bake, but I can do it tomorrow. How many people are coming?

audio.speaker: Jake
audio.text: Five, maybe six. The problem is we only have four chairs.

audio.speaker: Lina
audio.text: The lounge on the second floor has folding chairs. Just sign them out at the front desk.

audio.speaker: Jake
audio.text: Perfect. I'll go down there now before the desk closes.

questions.stem: Why does Lina change her plans?
options: The oven is broken
She wants to let Jake use the kitchen
She has to study for an exam
The front desk is closed
questions.explanation: She offers to bake tomorrow so Jake can cook tonight.

questions.stem: What will Jake do next?
options: Buy more chairs
Cancel the study group
Go to the front desk to borrow chairs
Move the group to the lounge
questions.explanation: Chairs must be signed out at the front desk, and he says he will go now.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor during office hours.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Professor Alvarez, I wanted to ask about the feedback on my essay. You wrote that my argument was 'descriptive rather than analytical.'

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Right. You summarized the three theories very accurately, but you never told me which one you found most convincing, or why.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: I thought we were supposed to stay neutral.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Neutral in tone, yes. But analysis means weighing the evidence. Even saying that one theory explains the early data better while another fits the later period would be a position.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: So I could revise the conclusion along those lines?

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Revise the body too. The comparison has to run through the whole essay, not just appear at the end.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness of the student's essay, according to the professor?
options: It contains factual errors about the theories
It fails to evaluate the theories it describes
It is written in an informal tone
It discusses too many theories
questions.explanation: He summarized accurately but never said which theory was most convincing — no evaluation.

questions.stem: What does the professor imply about the student's plan to revise only the conclusion?
options: It would be sufficient
It would not fully solve the problem
It would make the essay too long
It is not allowed after grading
questions.explanation: She says the comparison must run through the whole essay, not just appear at the end.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Hi, the catalog says the book I need is available, but it isn't on the shelf.

audio.speaker: Librarian
audio.text: Let me look. Ah, it was returned this morning, so it's probably still on a cart waiting to be shelved.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Is there any way to get it today? My paper is due tomorrow.

audio.speaker: Librarian
audio.text: I'll check the carts in the back. If I can't find it, there's an electronic version, but only one person can read it at a time.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: I'd prefer the print copy, but the e-book is fine if it's free right now.

questions.stem: Why is the book not on the shelf?
options: Another student has borrowed it
It has been returned but not yet put back
It was moved to the electronic collection
The catalog contains an error
questions.explanation: It was returned this morning and is likely on a cart waiting to be shelved.

questions.stem: What is the student's attitude toward the electronic version?
options: She refuses to use it
She would accept it as an alternative
She thinks it is more useful than the print copy
She is worried that it costs money
questions.explanation: She prefers print but says the e-book is fine if it is available.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between two students working on a group project.

audio.speaker: Ana
audio.text: I've been going through the survey responses, and something's off. Almost a third of people answered 'strongly agree' to every single question.

audio.speaker: Ben
audio.text: Even the reversed ones? Those were supposed to catch people who weren't reading carefully.

audio.speaker: Ana
audio.text: Exactly. So either we exclude them, or our results are going to look much more positive than they really are.

audio.speaker: Ben
audio.text: Excluding them makes our sample pretty small, though. Maybe we report the analysis both ways and explain the issue.

audio.speaker: Ana
audio.text: That's more honest. I'll run both versions tonight.

questions.stem: What problem have the students found?
options: Too few people answered the survey
Many respondents appear to have answered without reading
The survey questions were badly translated
The data file was lost
questions.explanation: Respondents agreed even with reversed items designed to detect careless answering.

questions.stem: Why does Ben suggest reporting the analysis both ways?
options: To make the project longer
Because excluding responses would reduce the sample considerably
Because the professor required it
To hide the problem from readers
questions.explanation: He notes that exclusion leaves a small sample, so presenting both analyses is a compromise.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation at the campus health center.

audio.speaker: Receptionist
audio.text: Good morning. Do you have an appointment?

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: No, I just need a flu shot. Is that possible without booking?

audio.speaker: Receptionist
audio.text: Flu shots are walk-in only on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Today's Wednesday, I'm afraid.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Oh. I have classes all day tomorrow until four.

audio.speaker: Receptionist
audio.text: We're open until six on Thursdays, so you could come right after class.

questions.stem: Why can't the student get a flu shot today?
options: The clinic has run out of vaccine
Walk-in shots are not offered on Wednesdays
He needs a doctor's note
The clinic is closing early
questions.explanation: Walk-ins are only on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and today is Wednesday.

questions.stem: What does the receptionist suggest?
options: Booking an appointment for next week
Coming on Thursday after four
Skipping his classes tomorrow
Going to a pharmacy instead
questions.explanation: The clinic is open until six on Thursdays, after his classes end at four.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between a graduate student and a lab manager.

audio.speaker: Lab manager
audio.text: I noticed you booked the microscope for twelve hours on Saturday.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Yes, my samples degrade quickly, so I need to image all of them on the same day.

audio.speaker: Lab manager
audio.text: I understand, but the policy caps weekend bookings at six hours so that other people get a turn. Could you prepare half the samples on Saturday and half on Sunday?

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: That would mean two separate batches, and then I can't compare them directly.

audio.speaker: Lab manager
audio.text: Fair enough. Send me a short note explaining that, and I'll ask the committee for an exception.

questions.stem: Why does the student object to splitting the work over two days?
options: She is not available on Sunday
Separate batches would make the comparison unreliable
The microscope is broken on Sundays
She has already prepared all the samples
questions.explanation: Two batches would prevent direct comparison of the samples.

questions.stem: What is the lab manager's final position?
options: He refuses the booking
He is willing to seek approval for the longer booking
He grants the booking without conditions
He suggests using a different microscope
questions.explanation: "I'll ask the committee for an exception" — he will request approval but cannot grant it himself.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bookstore employee.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Hi, I bought this textbook last week, but my professor just told us we're using the new edition.

audio.speaker: Employee
audio.text: We can exchange it as long as you have the receipt and the plastic wrap isn't opened.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Well, I did open it, but I haven't written in it.

audio.speaker: Employee
audio.text: Then I can't do a full exchange, but we can buy it back as a used book and give you store credit toward the new edition.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: I guess that's better than nothing.

questions.stem: Why can't the student receive a full exchange?
options: He lost his receipt
He has written in the book
The book's wrapping has been opened
The new edition is sold out
questions.explanation: A full exchange requires the wrap to be unopened; he opened it.

questions.stem: How does the student feel about the store's offer?
options: Delighted
Reluctantly accepting
Angry and unwilling
Confused about the terms
questions.explanation: "I guess that's better than nothing" expresses reluctant acceptance.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between two students after a lecture.

audio.speaker: Maya
audio.text: Did you follow the part about opportunity cost? I got lost when he brought up the farmer example.

audio.speaker: Leo
audio.text: Sort of. The idea is that the real cost of planting wheat isn't just seeds and labor. It's also the corn you could have grown on the same land instead.

audio.speaker: Maya
audio.text: So the cost is what you give up, not what you pay?

audio.speaker: Leo
audio.text: Both, really. But economists focus on what you give up, because that's what changes your decision.

audio.speaker: Maya
audio.text: That makes more sense. I should rewatch the recording before the quiz.

questions.stem: What are the students mainly discussing?
options: How to grow wheat efficiently
A concept from their economics lecture
The date of their next quiz
Why a farmer chose corn
questions.explanation: Leo explains opportunity cost, which Maya did not understand in the lecture.

questions.stem: Why does Leo mention corn?
options: To illustrate a forgone alternative
To show that corn is more profitable
To describe the professor's farm
To correct a mistake in the lecture
questions.explanation: Corn is the alternative given up by planting wheat — the opportunity cost.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the recreation center.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: I'd like to sign up for the beginner swimming class.

audio.speaker: Staff member
audio.text: The Monday class is full, but there are still spaces on Wednesday evenings.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Wednesday works. Do I need to bring anything?

audio.speaker: Staff member
audio.text: Just a swimsuit and a lock for the lockers. We provide towels and goggles.

questions.stem: Which class will the student probably join?
options: The Monday class
The Wednesday class
An advanced class
A class at another center
questions.explanation: Monday is full and she says Wednesday works.

questions.stem: What does the student need to bring?
options: Towels
Goggles
A lock
A membership card
questions.explanation: A swimsuit and a lock; towels and goggles are provided.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor about a research assistant position.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Thanks for applying. I'll be honest: you have less coding experience than the other candidates.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: That's true. But I've transcribed and coded about forty hours of interviews for my thesis, which I understand is most of this project.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: It is, actually. The programming part is relatively small, and frankly it's easier to teach than careful qualitative coding.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: I'd be happy to take an online course this summer to catch up.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: That would certainly help. Let me talk to my co-investigator, and I'll get back to you by Friday.

questions.stem: How does the student respond to the professor's concern?
options: She denies that she lacks coding experience
She highlights relevant experience that matches the main task
She withdraws her application
She asks for a different position
questions.explanation: She concedes the point but stresses her interview-coding experience, which is most of the project.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the professor's view of the student?
options: He has rejected her application
He now sees her as a stronger candidate than he first suggested
He thinks programming is the most important skill
He has already hired another candidate
questions.explanation: He agrees qualitative coding is harder to teach and welcomes her plan, suggesting improved prospects.

exercises.context: Listen to a conversation between two students planning a presentation.

audio.speaker: Omar
audio.text: We have twelve minutes, and right now our slides would take at least twenty.

audio.speaker: Sara
audio.text: The background section is the longest. Most of the class already knows that material.

audio.speaker: Omar
audio.text: True, but the professor said she wants to see that we understand the context.

audio.speaker: Sara
audio.text: Then let's keep one background slide and put the rest in a handout. That frees up time for our own results.

audio.speaker: Omar
audio.text: Good compromise. I'll draft the handout tonight.

questions.stem: What problem are the students trying to solve?
options: Their presentation is too long
They have no results yet
The professor rejected their topic
They disagree about who should speak
questions.explanation: Their slides would take twenty minutes but they only have twelve.

questions.stem: Why does Omar initially hesitate to cut the background section?
options: He wrote most of it
The professor wants evidence that they understand the context
The class has not studied the material
The handout would be too expensive
questions.explanation: He recalls that the professor wants to see their understanding of the context.
